title: The hidden price of free
text: The most profitable word in the digital economy is 'free'. We {{1}} nothing for search engines, maps and video calls, and we have quietly concluded that the internet runs on generosity. In reality, the largest companies on Earth sit {{2}} in the business of selling attention. When you are not paying, as the saying {{3}}, you are not the customer but the product. Your clicks, pauses and midnight searches are {{4}} into a profile that predicts what you will buy, watch and believe, and those predictions are auctioned to advertisers in {{5}} of a second. None of this is illegal, and much of it is {{6}} useful: free maps really did beat the paper versions, and free video calls changed family life. The trouble is subtler. Systems built to hold attention do not distinguish between the attention {{7}} on a documentary and the attention swallowed by outrage, so the feed quietly fills with whatever {{8}} hardest. 'Free', in other words, has a price; it is simply charged somewhere you cannot see.

gaps.explanation: 'we pay nothing for' — the collocation for spending money on something.
'sit squarely in the business of' — completely and directly.
'as the saying goes' — the fixed phrase for introducing a proverb; the other verbs do not perform that role.
'distilled into a profile' — condensed to its essence; dilute, drain and spill thin out or lose.
'in fractions of a second' — the fixed expression for tiny parts of time.
'much of it is genuinely useful' — truly; the manner adverbs describe how, not how much.
'the attention spent on a documentary' — spend + on.
'whatever hits hardest' — has the strongest effect.
